title: The miracle of the Qur'an
hook: a challenge sits inside the book itself: bring one surah like it

segments.voice: Yesterday, sifat, the attributes: hearing, seeing, knowing, willing, and your line: nothing like him. Which attribute did you sit with? Today the theologians' part ends with a book. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

A book usually asks to be believed. This one sets a test. In the second surah, al-Baqarah, the Qur'an turns to anyone who doubts where it came from and says, in Pickthall's translation: "then produce a surah of the like thereof, and call your witness beside Allah if ye are truthful." Not the whole book. One surah. The challenge is printed on the page, in the middle of the text it's defending, and it is read aloud whenever that surah is recited. Today's word is the name Muslim scholars gave to what they saw in that challenge.
screen: `A BOOK THAT SETS A TEST.` → `PRODUCE A SURAH LIKE IT.` → `THE CHALLENGE IS ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: The word is i'jaz. Lane's old Arabic lexicon puts it under a root about being unable, falling short. A mu'jizah, a miracle, is a sign that leaves others unable to match it. Musa had his staff. 'Isa, in the Qur'an, healed the blind. So what was the sign given to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his own answer, in paraphrase: every prophet was given signs that led people to believe, and what I was given is revelation that Allah revealed to me. The miracle, Muslims say, is the book. Another verse widens the challenge. Pickthall again: "though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another." Then the theologians we've spent these days with got to work, and they did not all agree. What exactly can't be matched? Some, like the scholar al-Baqillani, who wrote a whole book on i'jaz, pointed to its eloquence, which he held was beyond the reach of Arabic poetry. Others, like al-Jurjani, pointed to its nazm, the way its words are joined and arranged. Some also pointed to what the Qur'an tells of things unseen. And one Mu'tazili thinker, al-Nazzam, is remembered for a different answer: people could have matched it, but Allah turned them away from trying. Other scholars rejected that view, but it shows how seriously the question was taken. So this part ends where it began, with kalam: faith asking questions of its own book. And notice one thing. A staff or a healing is seen once. A book can be opened again tomorrow.
screen: `I'JAZ: LEAVING OTHERS UNABLE.` · `EACH PROPHET'S SIGN, AND THIS ONE A BOOK.` · `ELOQUENCE, ARRANGEMENT, OR TURNING AWAY?` · then, large: `A SIGN YOU CAN OPEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: recite one verse aloud. Choose one you know. Al-Fatiha's opening line, or al-Ikhlas, or, if you don't know any in Arabic, the line from al-Baqarah we heard today, in English. Settle, and breathe. Then say it out loud, slowly, at a normal speaking voice, not a whisper. Listen to the sounds as they leave you. Say it a second time, slower. Then sit in the quiet it leaves behind, and let the last word ring for a moment. The bell holds the time.
I'jaz. The inimitability of the Qur'an: the teaching that its words can't be matched, which Muslims hold as the Prophet's sign. Today's word.

Your line: the book as sign. Today, read one verse of any scripture as if it were addressed to you on purpose, and notice one word you'd usually skip. Tomorrow, a new part begins: death and return. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of the Qur'an as the Prophet's lasting miracle, and scholars of Arabic rhetoric and theology have written works on i'jaz, studying what in its language and arrangement they hold cannot be matched.

original.note: Arabic: inimitability, from a root about being unable or falling short.

trapdoor: what you thought: the miracle of the Qur'an means a miraculous event in the Prophet's life.
what it means: Muslims hold the book itself as the sign, one whose challenge, bring one surah like it, sits on its own pages.
what a scholar hears: i'jaz and mu'jizah, signs that leave others unable; and a debate between eloquence, nazm and al-Nazzam's turning away.
